lessons.title: Averages: mean, median, mode and range
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Mathematics; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate the mean (average) of a set of numbers.
Find the median, the mode and the range.
Use the mean to solve problems.
reviewNotes: Median for an even number of values may be left out by the school; it is mentioned briefly.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Mean
blocks.md: The **mean** (or average) = **total ÷ number of items**. The marks 12, 16, 9 and 14 add up to 51; there are 4 marks; the mean is 51 ÷ 4 = 12.75. The mean can be a decimal, and it need not be one of the numbers.

blocks.caption: The marks of four pupils out of 20.
blocks.alt: A bar chart: Ako 12, Bih 16, Che 9, Dina 14 marks out of 20.

blocks.title: Median, mode and range
blocks.md: Put the numbers in **order**. The **median** is the **middle** number (for 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 it is 7; with two middle numbers, take the number halfway between). The **mode** is the number that appears **most often**. The **range** is the **biggest minus the smallest**: for 9, 12, 14, 15 it is 15 − 9 = 6.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Dividing by the wrong number: divide by the **number of items**, not by the biggest value.
- Not putting the numbers in order before finding the median.
- Saying that there is no mode when two numbers tie (both are modes).
- Mixing range and mean.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Find the mean mark of the four pupils: 12, 16, 9, 14.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Find the median, mode and range of 4, 7, 4, 9, 6, 4, 8.
steps: Order: 4, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9. The middle (4th) number is 6. The number 4 appears 3 times.

objectives: Use words such as impossible, unlikely, likely and certain.
Write the probability of an event as a fraction.
List the possible outcomes of simple experiments.
reviewNotes: Probability is only an introduction (equally likely outcomes).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Chance
blocks.md: **Probability** tells how likely something is. An event can be **impossible** (cannot happen), **unlikely**, **even chance**, **likely** or **certain** (must happen). Probability is a number from **0** (impossible) to **1** (certain). Examples: the sun rising tomorrow is certain; a goat flying is impossible.

items.text: A bag: 3 red and 2 green marbles

blocks.caption: A bag with 3 red and 2 green marbles.
blocks.alt: A box with three red and two green marbles. Below, the probability of red is 3 over 5 and of green is 2 over 5.

blocks.title: Counting outcomes
blocks.md: If all outcomes are **equally likely**: probability = (number of ways the event can happen) ÷ (total number of outcomes). With 3 red and 2 green marbles there are 5 equally likely marbles, so P(red) = $\frac{3}{5}$. A fair coin has 2 outcomes: heads or tails, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing the probability as more than 1 (it cannot be).
- Counting only the favourable outcomes and not the total.
- Thinking that after 3 heads a coin is 'due' tails: each toss is independent.
- Confusing 'unlikely' with 'impossible'.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A bag has 3 red and 2 green marbles. What is the probability of taking a red marble?

items.text: A bag: 3 red and 2 green marbles

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A fair dice is rolled. What is the probability of getting an even number?
steps: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 favourable outcomes out of 6.

lessons.title: Profit, loss and percentage profit
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Mathematics; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Say what cost price and selling price are.
Find the profit or loss as a percentage of the cost price.
reviewNotes: Percentage profit is based on cost price, as is usual in school books; check local convention.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Profit and loss
blocks.md: The **cost price (CP)** is what the trader pays to buy goods. The **selling price (SP)** is what the trader sells them for. If SP is **more** than CP there is a **profit**: profit = SP − CP. If SP is **less** than CP there is a **loss**: loss = CP − SP.

blocks.caption: Profit and loss examples.
blocks.alt: A table with cost price, selling price and result: 5,000 to 6,500 is a profit of 1,500; 8,000 to 7,000 is a loss of 1,000.

blocks.title: Percentage profit
blocks.md: Percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100. If a trader buys for 5,000 FCFA and sells for 6,500 FCFA, the profit is 1,500 FCFA and the percentage profit is 1,500 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 30%. Always divide by the **cost price**, not by the selling price.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Dividing the profit by the selling price.
- Mixing profit and loss: check which price is bigger.
- Forgetting the unit FCFA.
- Forgetting that profit is not the same as the money received.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A trader buys a sack of rice for 18,000 FCFA and sells it for 21,000 FCFA. Find the profit.
steps: SP is bigger than CP, so there is a profit.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Find the percentage profit in Example 1.

lessons.title: Simple interest (introduction)
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Mathematics; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Say what principal, rate, time and interest are.
Calculate simple interest with the formula.
Find the total amount after some years.
reviewNotes: Interest and 'njangi' are mentioned as examples; whether the curriculum includes simple interest in Class 5 is to be checked (it may be Class 6).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Interest
blocks.md: When you **save** or **borrow** money, a bank or a savings group (njangi) may pay or charge **interest**. The money saved or borrowed is the **principal (P)**. The **rate (R)** is the percentage per year. The **time (T)** is the number of years. **Simple interest** is the same amount each year.

blocks.caption: An example of simple interest.
blocks.alt: A table: principal 50,000 FCFA, rate 5 per cent a year, time 2 years, interest 5,000 FCFA.

blocks.title: Formula
blocks.md: Simple interest $I = \frac{P \times R \times T}{100}$. Example: P = 50,000 FCFA, R = 5%, T = 2 years: I = 50,000 × 5 × 2 ÷ 100 = 5,000 FCFA. The **amount** at the end = principal + interest = 55,000 FCFA.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to divide by 100.
- Using months instead of years.
- Giving only the interest when the question asks for the total amount.
- Thinking the interest grows each year (that is compound interest, not studied here).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Find the simple interest on 50,000 FCFA at 5% a year for 2 years.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: What is the total amount after those 2 years?
